\section{Scenarios for the Lending Environment}
\label{sec:scenarios}

This section answers RQ3.
We compare the benchmark with three arms: bureau visibility alone, mandatory screening alone, and both together, which tests whether either switch changes the effect of the other.
The benchmark is the position before the reporting arrangements, in which \ac{BNPL} obligations are invisible to the bureau and requests pass only a light screen.
That light screen is a modelling assumption; whether an agreement that levies late fees is incidental credit, and which provisions would then apply, is a legal question the scenarios do not settle (Section~\ref{sec:background}).
Under bureau visibility, \ac{BNPL} obligations enter the traditional lender's Regulation 23A test, the affordability channel of the reported arrangements \cite{businessday_bnpl_2026}.
Under mandatory screening, the same test is applied to each \ac{BNPL} request, a stricter counterpart of the \ac{FCA}'s affordability check \cite{fca_ps26_1, woolard2021}.
Every arm is run at $\beta = 0$ and $\beta = 1$, with one hundred replications on shared seeds (Section~\ref{sec:sim-params}).
Differences are arm less benchmark at the same $\beta$, taken seed by seed.
We report cumulative volume beside default because a rule that only delays borrowing within the horizon leaves volume unchanged, whereas a rule that prevents borrowing lowers it.

Bureau visibility raises default, and screening does not change it detectably (Tables~\ref{tab:scenarios} and~\ref{tab:switches}; Figure~\ref{fig:scenarios}).

The rise under bureau visibility is $0.22 \pm 0.04$ points at $\beta = 0$ and $0.15 \pm 0.04$ at $\beta = 1$.
At $\beta = 0$ it is comparable to the $0.12 \pm 0.05$ by which enabling \ac{BNPL} raises default (Section~\ref{sec:results-injection}); the difference, $0.10 \pm 0.06$ points on different seeds, is not detectable.
Screening changes default by $+0.02 \pm 0.05$ and $+0.02 \pm 0.06$ points, so an effect of about a tenth of a point in either direction cannot be ruled out.
With both switches default is $0.10 \pm 0.05$ and $0.11 \pm 0.05$ points above the benchmark, each just beyond two standard errors.

Bureau visibility changes only the traditional lender's test, so it acts through that lender's refusals.
Once \ac{BNPL} obligations enter the Regulation 23A test, the lender refuses more applications, 1{,}388 against 1{,}190 at $\beta = 0$, and grants R4.97 million in place of R5.39 million.
The 90+ day arrears share among credit-active households rises by $0.42 \pm 0.05$ points at $\beta = 0$ and by $0.28 \pm 0.04$ at $\beta = 1$.
The rise in default is largest in Q1, at $0.59 \pm 0.07$ and $0.46 \pm 0.08$ points at $\beta = 0$ and $\beta = 1$.
It is not detectable in Q2 to Q4, and in Q5 it is $0.23 \pm 0.10$ and $0.22 \pm 0.11$ points, just beyond two standard errors.
A household that the lender refuses leaves its shortfall unpaid and is recorded as distressed (Section~\ref{sec:amount}), which is consistent with these rises.
Cumulative \ac{BNPL} volume is $2.6 \pm 0.6$\% lower at $\beta = 0$, although the switch does not act on \ac{BNPL} requests.

The model's rules may favour this result.
In the benchmark the lender lends the whole remaining shortfall, repayable over 25 months, on the household's surveyed income, and a household it refuses has no other source of credit.
A refusal therefore causes distress at once, while the cost of a granted loan is spread over 25 months and falls partly after the two-year run.
The switch was not run under the alternative borrowing rules of Table~\ref{tab:effect} or over a longer horizon.
The result gives the direction of the affordability channel under these rules and does not forecast the effect of the reporting arrangements.

Screening slightly lowers \ac{BNPL} holding and volume.
Holding at the final tick falls from 17.54\% to 15.69\% at $\beta = 0$ and from 66.74\% to 64.11\% at $\beta = 1$, and cumulative volume is $3.9 \pm 0.5$\% lower at $\beta = 0$ and $1.1 \pm 0.2$\% lower at $\beta = 1$.
The screening test already sees the household's \ac{BNPL} instalments and arrears on every platform (Section~\ref{sec:asymmetry}), so adding bureau visibility to screening gives the platforms no new information.
Bureau visibility then acts only on the traditional lender, and at $\beta = 0$ screening roughly halves its effect.
With both switches the lender refuses 114 more applications than in the benchmark, against 198 under bureau visibility alone, and default is $0.12 \pm 0.04$ points lower than under bureau visibility alone.
At $\beta = 1$ the two arms do not differ detectably.

Three features of the model may explain why screening alone does not change default.
A \ac{BNPL} agreement is small beside the room that the Regulation 23A test allows: each platform limits a household to a tenth of its monthly income and the mean want-driven purchase is R633, itself below the market figure (Section~\ref{sec:data-validation}), so the test refuses only households already close to its limit.
The test assesses affordability at origination on the household's surveyed income, whereas sustained distress in the model follows income shocks that arrive later and outlast the household's buffer (Section~\ref{sec:results-robustness}).
The traditional lender also stands behind the platforms: a shortfall request that screening refuses passes in full to the lender (Algorithm~\ref{alg:gate}), whereas one that the lender refuses under bureau visibility goes unmet.
None of these explanations is tested, because the outcomes do not follow the screened households.

Peer influence raises default by 0.53 to 0.61 points in every arm, but the comparisons give no evidence that it alters the effect of either switch: the effect of bureau visibility at $\beta = 1$ does not differ detectably from that at $\beta = 0$ ($-0.07 \pm 0.06$ points).

Two further levers, each run at both values of $\beta$, are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:levers}: a cooling-off window of one to four ticks after a want-driven purchase, and a cap on the number of platforms a household may owe, which no jurisdiction imposes.
Neither changes default detectably at $\beta = 0$; at $\beta = 1$ every window and caps of one and two lower default by 0.28 to 0.39 points.

In answer to RQ3, bureau visibility leads the traditional lender to refuse more applications and raises default by 0.15 to 0.22 points, with the largest rise in the lowest income quintile.
Mandatory screening slightly lowers \ac{BNPL} holding and volume and on its own does not change default detectably; added to bureau visibility at $\beta = 0$, it lowers default by $0.12 \pm 0.04$ points relative to bureau visibility alone.
